can effectively model discrete languages like English, but these models
primarily rely on English being modeled as a continuous space from which
discrete words are sampled. In contrast, our work explores the idea that
GANS can learn a continuous representation of language without the need
for intermediate continuous steps, instead directly modeling a space from
which pure words are sampled without any sampling process at all.
  To achieve this, we developed the Independent Token Generator (ITG),
which posits that a part-of-speech and word-specific parameters are
independently sampled from latent spaces, allowing a decoder to accurately
generate tokens in a zero-shot manner. Our results indicate that this
modeling approach not only outperforms previously established methods
using the GAN framework but also matches the performance of the most
advanced language modeling techniques, including NLP applications that
involve zero-shot language generation. Furthermore, our model can be
trained end-to-end without any specialized training, which significantly
reduces complexity. Our analysis demonstrates that the part-of-speech
independence is crucial to the success of this modeling approach and that
these GAN models have a notable similarity to recent breakthroughs in
advanced language models in terms of their linguistic representations. 
  Building upon this discovery, we developed the Compositional Token
Generator (CTG), which leverages syntactic structures by having a
dependency parsing-based sampling mechanism for both part-of-speech and
word-specific parameters from latent spaces, resulting in improved
performance. Notably, CTG matches the performance of ITG when using a
similar training approach but significantly outperforms it when
incorporating the structural information, demonstrating the positive
contribution of this information to the quality of the language model.
  To further evaluate the effectiveness of these models in generating
discrete language, we conducted an analysis of their linguistic
characteristics, such as word distribution and part-of-speech distribution,
and discovered that they possess many real-world similarities, which
considerably surpasses the performance of a basic language model. 
  Moving forward, we plan to explore the potential of these GAN-based
models for various NLP applications and to investigate the capacity of
these models for more intricate linguistic structures, such as syntactic
combinations, to further improve their linguistic representations and
overall language modeling performance. In addition, we have made our code
available at https://github.com/ghuli4/ITG-CT

discrete sections: setup, development, and punchline. 
  Typically, a joke begins by introducing its central idea or premise through a setup, then develops it by adding more detail or a supplementary idea, and finally concludes by combining these elements to create the humor. 
  This structure suggests a sequential writing approach could be effective, but it's also possible to employ a more flexible method, revising jokes in a non-sequential manner. 
  Research has demonstrated that experienced joke writers tend to create jokes in a fixed order, yet still frequently revise their work in an iterative process. 
  This study investigates the benefits of a particular revision technique known as "flipping," where the development and punchline sections of a joke are swapped, and its effects on creating novel jokes using this method. 
  Flipping was found to enhance the original joke's rating when applied to jokes rated highly by others, yet resulted in unimproved or slightly lower ratings for jokes rated poorly. 
  Additionally, analysis shows that this technique is most effective for jokes in which the setup, when rewritten, results in a development section more suitable to the premise, and is most likely to produce positive outcomes when the punchline can be easily integrated into the revised development. 
  Overall, this research indicates that joke revision through flipping can positively impact the quality of jokes, and may be particularly valuable for joke writers struggling with their punchlines. 
  This study also contributes to our understanding of the cognitive processes involved in creative writing by shedding light on the reversibility of revisions. 
  Finally, various practical strategies have been derived for joke writers, and additional techniques could be developed in the future by further exploring the findings of this research. 
  Additional experiments have also been proposed to further investigate the potential of this study. 
  Finally, this research has been implemented in the form of an interactive tool called JOKER, which enables joke writers to utilize revision techniques like flipping to generate more creative jokes. 
  This tool has already shown promise in producing novel, highly-rated jokes in a range of joke types, and has the potential to be further developed and expanded upon in the future. 
  This research has already received recognition at international conferences, such as ACL and IJCAI, and has been accepted for publication in prominent journals including Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics and Artificial Intelligence. 
  This research has already resulted in one accepted paper and an additional paper is currently under review, and has the potential to generate further publications in the future.

It's only recently, with the emergence of digital technologies, that art has begun to take on a more objective purpose - to contribute to scientific advancements and international cooperation. This shift has given rise to a new category of artworks known as "science art," characterized by their integration in the scientific process and widespread global distribution. As this field continues to grow, it poses challenges for artists, scientists, and institutions in terms of understanding its definition, scope, and the roles that different stakeholders play. This paper aims to clarify the definition, values, and roles associated with science art, drawing from the experiences of the ZIKV Artist-in-Residence program at the Max Planck Institute for Infection Biology and the role of art in the scientific process more broadly. 

  The program brought together visual artists with scientists working on the Zika virus, allowing them to explore common topics and develop new perspectives on their research. This unique collaboration not only facilitated a more comprehensive grasp of the subject but also yielded various forms of art, as shown in Figure 1, which served as a means for scientists to communicate their findings to a wider audience and ultimately contributed to public understanding. As a result, we believe that science art should be defined by its integration in the scientific process, the diversity of methods and media used by artists, and its ability to bring about lasting impacts - whether tangible or intangible - that extend beyond the initial creation itself. 

  Science art is a collaborative effort involving artists, scientists, and other stakeholders, each of whom contributes unique values. Artists benefit from the opportunity to engage with emerging topics and topics that are often considered sensitive or taboo, while scientists gain a more accessible means of communicating their research and exploring new perspectives. Institutions, on the other hand, are able to promote public understanding of science and its numerous applications. In light of these mutual benefits, we believe that science art should be supported and its diverse outcomes displayed in various settings, as a means of promoting its significance and promoting further development in the field. 

  Finally, we reflect on the challenges and opportunities presented by the various platforms and settings in which science art is showcased. While temporary exhibitions and online platforms have the advantage of flexibility and reach, they often lack the immersive quality provided by more permanent installations or real-world settings such as public gardens. Ultimately, we hope that science art will continue to evolve and address pressing scientific and societal issues, serving as a means of expression, communication

Traditional methods for handling adversarial examples require significant scaling factors, making them impractical for streaming applications. Our research focuses on classification algorithms for a limited number of classes, and we develop the first streaming algorithm capable of accurately classifying linear classifiers, even in the presence of adversarial examples. Our approach assumes a bounded input density, allowing it to accurately classify up to a specified error margin. The proposed algorithm operates in O(d log^2 D) space and O(d log^3) time, where d represents dimensionality and D is the data size. This exceeds the space requirements for streaming algorithms in standard settings, but is more feasible given the prior knowledge of data size. Our results also demonstrate that accurate classification is only possible if the classifier's weight vectors meet a specific condition and have bounded spectral norm. The proposed algorithm can be easily modified for kernelized linear classifiers, utilizing a random Fourier feature technique to overcome the dimensionality issues. This kernelized algorithm operates in O(d) space and O(d log^2 D) time, and is the first of its kind to provide accurate classifications in the presence of adversarial examples. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of these approaches, and highlight their potential for use in machine learning and networking applications. Our research combines the principles of streaming algorithms and robust learning, and provides a unique contribution to the field of machine learning and networking.

, the concept of length contraction is a fundamental aspect. However, this idea often leads people to believe that objects appear shorter when moving at a high speed, which is only partially correct. When considering a full assessment, the situation becomes more complex.

  A key point to understand is that the perceived lengths of objects are not fixed and can vary depending on the observer's frame of reference. Objects can appear longer or shorter, not just shorter, based on the relative motion between the observer and the object. 

  A classic example helps to illustrate this concept. If a car is driving at a high speed and you're viewing it from the side, it will appear shorter due to length contraction. However, if you were inside the car, looking out the back, the situation would be different. In this case, the car would appear longer than usual because the width is now being projected onto the vertical dimension. 

  Similarly, objects can also appear longer than usual when viewed from a moving frame of reference. This counterintuitive effect is just as much a part of Special Relativity as length contraction and deserves recognition. By incorporating these complexities, we can strive for a more comprehensive and accurate understanding of relativity, moving beyond simplistic misconceptions along the way. 

  Ultimately, the goal is not only to memorize key formulas but also to develop a deep and nuanced understanding of the underlying principles, even if it takes time to reconcile any initial intuitive misconceptions with the actual facts.  A final thought, relativity is not just about making objects appear shorter when moving at high speeds; it's about embracing a more complete and consistent description of the universe, one that incorporates time and space in a unified way.  When approached with patience and an open mind, relativity can be a rich and rewarding subject to explore. In this study, we examine the minimal amount of memory and work necessary to achieve a specified relative residual in solving a 2D Helmholtz equation using an iterative multigrid method. on the development and behavior of vortices and quasiparticles in a system that includes bosons and fermions, specifically in a type-II Bose-Fermi superfluid. When a magnetic field with a specific orientation is applied, it causes the formation of bound states consisting of a bosonic vortex and two adjacent fermionic quasiparticles. This bound state moves cohesively with the application of an external force. By using a mathematical framework that incorporates both semi-classical and weakly-linked approximations, we are able to investigate the consequences of the magnetic field on this phenomenon. Our research reveals how the magnetic field affects the formation and movement of the bound state, particularly in systems that are influenced by a type-II Bose-Fermi phase transition. In this study, we develop a method to identify the underlying values of a society by using a unique approach called "revealed preference analysis." By analyzing how individuals trade off one good against another, we can infer their relative priorities. Typically, researchers rely on how people spend their income or time, but we propose a more versatile approach. Instead, we ask how people react to changes in various social issues, such as access to healthcare or education. Our results show that people's values prioritize equal healthcare and education over extensive economic growth, and our method provides a more comprehensive understanding of a society's values than traditional methods, offering valuable insights for policymakers and researchers. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to a wide range of decision-making scenarios, such as how a government prioritizes the development of different industries or the distribution of taxes. By providing a more accurate measure of a society's values, we can make more informed decisions about how to achieve the best possible social outcomes. Our study demonstrates the feasibility of using revealed preference analysis to inform policy decisions in various real-world contexts. Using a Boltzmann equation-based method, we derive the coefficients of the model, specifically the shear viscosity, bulk viscosity, and thermal conductivity. Additionally, we outline strategies for applying the model in situations with non-zero external forces and expanding it to include bulk viscous effects and long-range interactions. To illustrate the model's capabilities, we simulate a range of non-relativistic and relativistic hydrodynamic phenomena, such as shear shower, jet propagation, and expanding fireballs, with the model showing promising results and generally agreement with existing data. The model is found to effectively describe both bulk and shear flows at low and high values of Lorentz factor, with bulk viscous effects evident in specific situations. Overall, the model holds great promise for a broad range of applications, from astrophysics to heavy-ion collisions. Moreover, we outline potential connections with other hydrodynamic models, such as kinetic and causal hydrodynamic models, as well as future extensions with a causal Einstein theory and fluid and heat carriers. Finally, we outline the challenges and future directions for the model, specifically simulation of ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions with a causal Einstein theory and fluid and heat carriers. treating all classes equally can lead 
  to overemphasizing the minority classes at the expense of the majority. This 
  results in poor generalization performance on unseen data. Active learning, 
  which involves selecting specific examples for annotation, can further exacerbate 
  the issue if not managed properly. Therefore, developing methods that effectively 
  address class imbalance has become crucial for creating more generalizable active 
  learning systems. One method involves utilizing a query-by-commitment approach, 
  which allows the selection of easy-to-classify examples and thus minority-class 
  overfitting. This can be achieved by incorporating a penalty term in the proposed 
  data-balancing approach to discourage minority-class overfitting. Experimental 
  results demonstrate the importance of addressing class imbalance in active learning 
  and the proposed method outperforms traditional methods. Additionally, the code 
  associated with this research will be publicly available for further verification. 
  This study also includes an in-depth analysis of multiple active learning strategies 
  incorporating data balancing techniques. Ultimately, the goal is to create more 
  efficient active learning systems capable of generalizing effectively to unseen data.  

  This research was inspired by a conversation with Dr. Alex Kossovsky, who initially 
  suggested addressing class imbalance in active learning. Further insights were gained 
  from Dr. Alex's work and the related projects by Sebastian Bader and Eric Paquet. 
  Additionally, I would like to extend my gratitude to the members of the IVLAB research 
  center for their invaluable feedback and support. 

  As an active learner myself, I would like to express my appreciation to the many 
  individuals who provided insightful feedback on this research, which has been ongoing 
  for two years and has yielded significant progress. 

  Finally, I would like to acknowledge the generous support provided by the IV 
  foundation, which facilitated the completion of this research. 

  In terms of future work, I plan to explore the potential of developing active 
  learning systems capable of balancing classes in real-time. This could involve 
  selecting examples that are not only easily classifiable but also reflective of 
  the distribution of the training set. 

  One potential approach to achieving this goal involves utilizing a query-by-commitment 
  strategy, which allows the selection of specific examples for annotation based 
  on their potential to improve the model's generalization performance. 

  Another method involves incorporating a data balancing approach to address the issue 
  of class imbalance.

University of Edinburgh's team for the 2022 Inner workings of the Web (IWoW) challenge. The objective of IWoW is to uncover hidden patterns in a graph representing hypertext documents, whereas previous approaches focused on linking structure. Our strategy involves employing pre-trained language models to generate both node and edge descriptions, which are then fed into multi-layer perceptrons. The descriptions are produced by combining textual information with semantic data like RDF and page ranking. The selected features are able to capture both the physical and semantic characteristics of the Web pages, which are passed on to the linking models. The linking models are trained on human-edited Wikipedia pages and produce hard predictions by selecting the most probable outgoing links. The node representation models are trained on large-scale graph representations and employ language model encodings as input. The overall system is trained end-to-end on a custom graph representing Web pages. The experimental results show our method to be competitive with the current best approaches in both novel and semi-eval tasks. The proposed models benefit from the combined strengths of language and graph models, as well as large training datasets. To achieve this, we utilize the standardized codepoints of the Unicode character set, allowing a single neural network to cover all languages recognized by the standard.   This study presents a groundbreaking development in the deep learning community by designing a neural model capable of processing texts in languages that use non-ASCII characters. Unlike previous models, which are typically tailored to specific languages, the proposed model is intended to be universally applicable to all languages recognized by the Unicode standard. To achieve this, the model encodes non-ASCII characters into a standardized codepoint, allowing a single neural network to be trained on multiple languages efficiently. Our approach is unique in that it possesses a unified and flexible representation of text, and we demonstrate through experiments that the model outperforms language-specific models by a substantial margin while also exhibiting improved memory efficiency. Furthermore, the proposed model is capable of identifying consistent language characteristics across individual words and has been successful in adhering to these patterns through statistical analysis. Lastly, the model presents an opportunity for significant memory savings, estimated to be a factor of 10, and is expected to have a far-reaching impact on the development of future machine learning systems.

primordial black holes (PBHs) could make up a significant portion of the total mass. If these ancient objects are created during specific phases of the Universe's development, they might be detectable in specific waves of gravitational radiation. This text explores the link between certain types of gravitational waves and the proposed PBHs, considering two distinct scenarios. The first involves wave patterns with irregular durations, which are potentially generated by the merger of smaller PBHs. The second examines the link between low-frequency gravitational waves and the proposed PBHs, focusing on an expansion theory. An analytical model based on a gas-like expansion is developed to estimate the predicted wave amplitude, and this model is compared to existing research. This text also discusses limitations and potential modifications to the proposed theory, and it explores alternative explanations for the observed gravitational waves. Furthermore, the feasibility of detecting these waves using current methods is assessed. If these waves are confirmed, several consequences emerge, including a revised estimate of the Universe's entropy density and potential impacts on the matter density, which could affect the formation of structure in the Universe. The proposed detection could also influence our understanding of the proposed PBHs, possibly limiting their mass range and reducing the likelihood that they comprise more than a certain percentage of the total mass. Finally, a detection might also facilitate the observation of smaller PBHs in high-energy particle collisions, including a notable phenomenon known as "microholes." On the other hand, a non-detection could relax these constraints, and it could also reduce the minimum mass for PBHs by several orders of magnitude, increasing their potential mass range. Several experimental and observational searches for these types of gravitational waves have been conducted in the past, and future projects could potentially provide significant evidence. In particular, one such project, called LIGO, has recently reported preliminary findings that could significantly influence our understanding of the proposed PBHs and the proposed alternative dark matter theories. Therefore, it is essential to coordinate research efforts to ensure that findings are interpreted consistently and to facilitate meaningful comparisons between different studies. To this end, a uniform set of standards for analyzing data is proposed, along with several key benchmarks for evaluating the proposed theories. These standards and benchmarks will facilitate consistent analysis of data and meaningful comparisons between different studies, and they will also ensure that proposed theories are adequately tested. Several key areas where proposed theories could be tested are identified, and it is particularly important to verify that proposed theories are not in conflict with established observations. A test of this type is particularly important for the proposed PBH theories,

Recent research on $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ has generated considerable interest among physicists due to its potential to exhibit QSL behavior beneath a surface-induced antiferromagnetic layer. To better comprehend the magnetic properties of this material, researchers have performed high-field magnetic structure and phase diagram studies. Combining neutron scattering and muon spin resonance spectroscopy, the team obtained evidence for a unique magnetic phase and identified its spin polarization. This discovery confirms that $\alpha$-RuCl$_3$ exhibits a Kitaev-like component in addition to an Ising-like component, presenting a complex interplay between the two. The obtained data suggest the presence of a QSL state and antiferromagnetic order near a critical point at around 10 Tesla. The nature of this ordered state remains ambiguous, with possible explanations of spin ice or a chiral QSL state. Ultimately, the magnetic properties of $\alpha$-RuCl_3 can be described using an effective spin model that incorporates the Kitaev, Heisenberg, and Ising interactions. The findings of this research will aid in understanding the magnetic phenomena in quantum spin systems and provide valuable insights into the properties of Kitaev materials. However, traditional MVS approaches are limited by their dependence on extensive human annotation to function properly.  This can be costly and impractical to obtain on large-scale systems.  Therefore, we propose a novel training method that allows MVS networks to generate 3D points directly from raw images, eliminating the need for annotated depth maps or voxels.  This method is based on the concept of observing a scene from multiple angles and using a pose-conditional approach to generate 3D points across various viewpoints.  Our approach also includes a novel type of 3D-3D supervision, where the network is trained to recognize a specific object regardless of changes in viewpoint, lighting, or other environmental factors.  By testing our method using a large, publicly available dataset of object sequences, we demonstrate a significant improvement in both reconstruction accuracy and generation speed compared to existing MVS models.  Additionally, the generated point clouds can function as a form of object-level representation for pose-conditioned object detection.  Therefore, we believe our method has the potential to revolutionize the field of MVS and related computer vision applications.  This method can also be seen as a form of extension to the more general concept of volume rendering, where the output is condensed into a more manageable 3D point cloud for easier use in various applications. This system, commonly employed in attempts to demonstrate the quantum-classical correspondence, presents challenges due to its non-switchable quantum components.  Consequently, there has been an ongoing quest for a suitable interpretation of quantum mechanics that can reconcile this model with the inherent randomness inherent to quantum mechanics.  Here, we re-examine the requirements for an interpretation, suggesting that any viable approach must first address the issues presented by this scenario and then, subsequently, those of the standard von Neumann interpretation.  In light of the influence of decoherence as a mechanism for maintaining internal coherence within the atom despite environmental interaction, our analysis is in line with the broader trend in proposals for quantum theories - a shift towards a focus on how measurements are utilized to eliminate irrelevant information from the system, rather than adhering to a strictly von Neumann-style approach centered on the objective assessment of global states. A key benefit of multi-tasking is its potential to leverage information across related tasks. Despite this, the amount of task overlap affects model performance in an inversely U-shaped manner. This counter-intuitive finding indicates that neither highly correlated nor highly distinct tasks yield optimal results. This discovery led us to design a novel adaptive method that adjusts the level of task overlap by regulating the amount of shared features learned. This is achieved through the introduction of a new regularization technique and a novel data augmentation method, both of which are tailored to minimize feature overlap between tasks. Experimental results on diverse datasets indicate that our method is as efficient as current methods and can successfully adjust task correlation to improve model performance. This method is particularly effective in ensemble learning and federated learning applications, where task correlation is difficult to control. To achieve these improvements, we developed a new adaptive data augmentation method that balances task-specific and shared features using optimal correlation coefficients. A thorough analysis of our method reveals its numerous benefits, including better generalization, increased robustness to out-of-distribution data, and improved model interpretability. This research shows that a wide range of existing multi-tasking methods can be enhanced by incorporating an adaptive data augmentation strategy. Finally, we explored the potential to extend our method to more complex scenarios, such as transfer learning, by using shared features between source and target domains as a bridge for knowledge transfer. b Cs optical atomic clocks are largely attributed to photon scattering, a phenomenon that occurs due to the interaction of light with the atoms. This scattering leads to a reduction in the number of usable atoms, thereby increasing the relative frequency uncertainty. To mitigate this issue, a novel optical clock concept has been proposed, utilizing a cold and dilute gas of strontium atoms confined within a micro-optical trap. By employing a specific trap design and optimizing the choice of strontium isotopes, a significantly reduced scattering probability was achieved, thereby making it feasible to maintain a large population of atoms even at high optical excitation amplitudes. This advancement has enabled the development of an ultra-precise frequency standard, yielding an unprecedented relative frequency uncertainty of approximately $5\times10^{-18}$. This breakthrough has paved the way for ground-based and space-based applications of optical clocks over the next decade. Moreover, the high-optical-excitation-clock (HOEC) concept has opened doors for future research in advanced atomic physics experiments, offering valuable insights into the interactions between light and matter. Finally, the long-term stability of the HOEC has been evaluated after ten years, considering several factors including improvements in laser technology, temperature fluctuations, and gravitational effects. This analysis has shown that, when these effects are accounted for, the relative frequency uncertainty of the HOEC will reach an extraordinary level of approximately $3\times10^{-18}$ in the future. Ultimately, the innovative ideas and methodologies developed within the framework of the HOEC could have a profound impact, potentially leading to breakthroughs in fundamental scientific studies and highly accurate timekeeping applications. Furthermore, the precise frequency stability of the HOEC has been calculated over various distances from the Sun, and upon launch of a clock into space, where gravitational effects are minimized, the relative frequency uncertainty is expected to drop dramatically to a remarkable level of approximately $1\times10^{-17}$. Finally, the potential for future space-based applications of optical clocks over the next two decades has been assessed, and when these clocks are launched into orbit around the Earth, the relative frequency uncertainty is expected to reach an extraordinary level of approximately $1\times10^{-18}$ and further to $2\times10^{-18}$ and $3\times10^{-19}$ for geostationary orbit, Sun orbit and Sun's center orbit respectively. Optical clocks have the potential to significantly advance our understanding of time and physics, and such exceptional tools could have a major impact, revolutionizing the fields of physics and timekeeping. Our goal is to examine how the number of distinct strategies evolved over multiple generations, while also considering the impact of varying the problem's level of difficulty. We aimed to replicate a phenomenon previously observed in mathematical research, in which the prevalence of certain approaches tends to decrease as the problem becomes more complex, yet ultimately increases once again. The existing CVAE and vae models have several limitations in producing zero-padded outputs, thereby hindering their practical applications. To address this issue, we developed a scCVAE model, which combines the concepts of hierarchical alpha-recursive neural networks and targeted noise removal. The proposed model comprises two primary components - a sparse conditional variational autoencoder and a sample generator. The former leverages a variational encoder and a decoder to learn a prior distribution of image sparse codes and a mapping from images to this prior distribution. The latter utilizes a generator network to produce a sample from the learned prior distribution. The model learns a common latent space for images and sparse codes by optimizing a lower bound of the data likelihood, thereby enabling the reconstruction of original images from sparse codes and vice versa. Experimental results on MNIST and Omniglot datasets validate the superior performance of the proposed scCVAE model in terms of sample quality and efficiency compared to the CVAE and vae models. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/zhixuhao/sccvae.  The model's capability to generate sparse codes allows for efficient representation of images, which in turn paves the way for efficient storage and processing of generated images. Furthermore, the model's ability to produce a prior distribution of sparse codes empowers a variety of downstream tasks, such as image generation, filling in missing pixels, and altering image attributes. With its superior performance and various practical applications, the proposed scCVAE model holds considerable potential for further research and development. Clouds that are too dense and isolated will eventually collapse under their own gravity, forming new stars, but only if they lack sufficient internal pressure to support themselves against the force of gravity.  Pressure within the cloud is generated by the movement of its constituent gas molecules, and this movement is characterized by its temperature and overall level of energy.  When this pressure is insufficient to counteract the force of gravity, the cloud collapses, forming new stars, and the resulting stars in turn have conditions that are too hot near the core and too cool near the edges, indicating that they drew their material from a single, rapidly-moving cloud rather than separate, high-energy sources.

  However, it is unclear whether these conditions are sufficient to explain the origin of the elements, particularly iron, within the core of the resulting stars. If the elements within the core of these stars are the result of a single, rapidly-moving cloud, this raises the further question of whether the elements within the core of these stars are part of a single, unified set, or whether they are the result of multiple separate processes.

Developing methods to accurately measure learning has therefore become a crucial aspect of both educational systems and adaptive, intelligent systems. In this study, the link between the confidence of human judgments and their accuracy is being investigated. We present a novel method for modeling the relationship between confidence and accuracy, and demonstrate its applicability in measuring learning through self-assessment. This method enables the detection of learning by analyzing changes in the link between confidence and accuracy over the course of a training or tutoring process. We illustrate its effectiveness using data from math tutoring sessions. Furthermore, we show that this method not only detects individuals who have learned but also identifies the learning achieved by each person. Unlike traditional detection methods, our approach produces a precise quantification of the impact of the tutoring on the learners' skills. The obtained results suggest a significant correlation between the reduction in subjective uncertainty and the improvement in performance, indicating that learners tend to reduce their subjective uncertainty more significantly than their actual uncertainty, thus exhibiting an overall decrease in confidence despite an overall increase in performance capability. These findings are consistent with the common phenomenon of improved performance and reduced confidence observed in learners. By analyzing both individual and group-level data, we reveal that learners can be categorized into three distinct categories based on their learning patterns. We also demonstrate that our proposed method enables the quantification of the degree of learning for each learner, and show that learners' performance and subjective uncertainty follow a similar pattern of improvement, although to a different extent. The obtained results indicate that our proposed method is effective for detecting learners, evaluating the impact of the tutoring on the learners' skills, and providing a detailed analysis of both individual and group-level performance. This study provides strong empirical support for the use of our proposed method in measuring learning through self-assessment. Moreover, we highlight the significance of our obtained results, and provide future directions for research by analyzing the differences between our approach and traditional methods for detecting learning. Existing solutions either offer high throughput but poor access times or fast access but low scalability, making them ill-suited for modern data analytics applications. To address this gap, we propose HiFi, a high-speed, flash-based storage architecture that combines the benefits of parallelism and chip-level bandwidth. By leveraging a flash array as a cache to disk arrays, HiFi allows multiple disks to be accessed in parallel, thereby achieving a seamless fusion of performance and capacity. Our experimental evaluations have demonstrated the efficacy of this approach, showcasing a specific storage system that can deliver 297,000 IOPS, offer up to 260 GB of capacity, and provide an overall average response time of just 10 microseconds. This includes a 3.5-fold improvement in IOPS, a 26-fold increase in scalability, and response times only slightly longer than a traditional disk-based storage system, thus validating the design and confirming the potential for a new generation of high-performance storage systems. Furthermore, our design is modular and adaptable, allowing it to be applied to various other storage architectures and thus empowering a wide range of innovative storage innovations. Additionally, our work includes a detailed performance model that can be used to predict and optimize various performance metrics in modern storage systems. This model includes a new formula for combining different access times and determining overall latency, as well as the ability to forecast system behavior under different workload patterns and configurations. By applying this model to our HiFi architecture, we were able to simulate and validate the performance of this new storage system before actual implementation, thereby validating our design and confirming the model's accuracy and usefulness. Furthermore, our model can be used to evaluate and compare the performance of different storage architectures, as shown in this work where various combinations of parallelism and depth are analyzed to determine the ideal configuration for the HiFi design. gaining attention as a promising alternative to traditional lithium-ion batteries. Despite this, there is a lack of computational methods to evaluate their potential. By storing frequently used content in switches along the data paths, we can lower request latency and decrease load on remote servers. Yet, this also introduces a security vulnerability as cached content can be accessed without authorization. To address this issue, we present a novel concept called C-Null, which allows switches to efficiently delete sensitive data promptly after a data session ends. C-Null achieves this by constructing a special deletion list for each data object when it's first transmitted over the network. When a session terminates, the switch simply deletes the object, and the server is notified to update the completion list; the switch then checks the next pending deletion on the list and deletes it if present. This process continues until the session ends, and the server is notified to update the list again. By centralizing deletion management, the switch never has to store multiple versions of data at once, reducing the risk of data exposure. Furthermore, we compare C-Null against an alternative solution, Null, which relies solely on centralized management to ensure data integrity. Through a combination of analytical modeling and simulations, we show that C-Null significantly outperforms Null in key metrics such as session completion latency and server overhead. Finally, we discuss the practical feasibility of implementing C-Null in actual caching systems. The results demonstrate that C-Null is both a secure and efficient solution for in-network caching.

Using idioms is a common way to add variety and clarity to language, but they often present challenges for machine translation. This paper explores the characteristics of translated texts that indicate whether an idiom has been successfully translated. By conducting an in-depth analysis of translated English and German texts, we identify several features that can be used to assess the accuracy of machine translation. These features include the typical length of idioms in each language, the presence of non-literal language, and the connections between words within idioms. Additionally, we show that successful translations are more likely to preserve the grammatical structure and the overall meaning of the original idiom. By examining these aspects, we gain a more comprehensive understanding of how machine translation deals with idioms and other complex expressions. This knowledge can be used to develop more effective methods for generating and evaluating machine translations. The accompanying code is available at https://github.com/jasellis/idiomatic_translation_features. "

While some studies limit their focus to two or three dimensions, other areas like medical and neurological studies require considering data with even higher temporal complexities.  Therefore, developing a reliable method for registering data across these varying dimensions is crucial.  Our approach, Probabilistic Component-Ordered Registration (PCOR), provides a flexible framework that captures the organization within high-dimensional data by breaking it down into interconnected components.  PCOR utilizes a probabilistic model to map the data onto a common framework, incorporating prior knowledge about the underlying structure through a multivariate normal distribution with constrained matricial parameters. The implementation of PCOR has been made publicly available on the Neuroimaging Analysis Tool website (natacortex.org). The primary challenge is creating a reliable and consistent gait signature that can accurately distinguish between different individuals. To address this, we will be comparing two techniques - one that produces a consistent gait signature and another that generates a consistent signature while also being difficult to replicate, effectively creating a secure gait signature. For the first technique, we will be controlling external factors to produce a consistent signature, while for the second, we will be manipulating the system to produce one. Furthermore, this research will be incorporating an efficient matching process, such as the RNSD, to verify individual identity. All experiments were approved by our institutional review board. 

  To produce a consistent gait signature, we collected data from multiple walks for each individual and combined these walks into different segments. We then extracted features from each segment and calculated the corresponding distances. To achieve a reliable verification, we used the cumulative distribution function to determine whether a given individual's gait matched another, accounting for any potential variations. Specifically, we set a threshold such that less than 1% of non-matches scored above it and less than 1% of matches scored below it. 

  In our first experiment, we analyzed how long it took to score a match or non-match for different segments, as well as how often errors occurred. The results showed that the most accurate scores came from the first 7 segments, with an error rate of 0.8% for non-matches and 0.4% of matches scoring below the threshold. We then conducted two additional experiments to determine the impact of different factors - one involved changing the length of the gait signature and the other adjusted the threshold. Both found that the performance improved over time but reached a plateau at a certain point for the first, and decreasing the threshold resulted in more accurate scores but at the cost of more non-matches scoring above it. 

  To produce a secure gait signature, we applied different techniques - modifying the length of the signature, altering the number of features used, and applying a form of encryption - and found that all resulted in improved performance. Specifically, adjusting the amount of data and features available reduced the accuracy but also significantly decreased the likelihood of non-matches scoring above the threshold, while encryption slightly increased this risk but had the most effective impact on this metric. Furthermore, modifying the signature through various methods also improved the secure performance, with the best results achieved when a certain amount of data was used.

This means there isn't a Banach space with an inherent continuity structure that allows for an isometric embedding of C[0,1]. This resolves an open question from the 2007 Banach space workshop and provides an added insight from an entropy perspective, highlighting that any Banach space with an approximate identity cannot serve as a uniform norm isometric embedding for C[0,1]. This discovery is also reflected in a similar failure for l^1 to be isometrically embeddable into any Banach space with an approximate identity. This failure is further attributed to a key entropy criterion proposed within this study, which is presented as Theorem 2.6 and has far-reaching consequences discussed in further research. A new model, known as the "information highway," has been created to facilitate the dissemination of research in developing areas.  Our study assesses the effectiveness of this model in enhancing dissemination by conducting a before-and-after analysis across seven universities in Nigeria.  A structured questionnaire was distributed to 304 academics before the introduction of the information highway and again after its implementation.  The results reveal a significant improvement in research output and a substantial increase in research productivity, with a substantial positive correlation observed.  Furthermore, the information highway's influence on research dissemination is found to be mediated by researchers' access to internet facilities and their overall proficiency in using digital technology.  Therefore, it can be concluded that the information highway successfully enhances research dissemination, particularly in the developing world, by bridging the information technology gap.  As such, it is highly recommended that universities in the developing world integrate this model into their existing strategies to improve research dissemination.  A call is also made for further research on the long-term effects of the information highway and similar initiatives aimed at enhancing research dissemination.  Additionally, the study identifies potential limitations that could impact the generalizability of its findings, including the reliance on subjective data and the reliance of academics on the internet for research dissemination.  Future studies are encouraged to explore these limitations and potential challenges in greater detail. This has the consequence of providing a uniform resolution of the singularities of the class of toroidal $d$-fold curves. Additionally, we establish that the set of exceptional divisors in the GND for any given toroidal $d$-fold variety is finite and that the corresponding set of exceptional prime ideals is also finite. This work heavily draws on and extends previously developed methods in the contexts of one-dimensional and two-dimensional cases. Furthermore, it involves the introduction of new and innovative techniques. Ultimately, this work aims to contribute to an extension of the GND to the broader category of varieties that are partially defined over the torus. Specifically, we propose that the set of exceptional prime ideals in the GND for any given toroidal $d$-fold variety should be independent of $d$ and that this set could serve as a toric parameterization obstruction, a concept that we term the GND obstruction. This GND obstruction is known to occur in the one-dimensional and two-dimensional cases and we argue that it should also occur for all higher dimensional cases. We also propose that varieties that are missing this obstruction - what we term GND-admissible varieties - are precisely those that can be equipped with a toroidal $d$-fold morphism to the torus. This relationship between GND-admissibility and torus-invariance has far-reaching implications that we explore here. One consequence is that the set of exceptional prime ideals in the GND for any given torus-invariant variety should be empty. This observation motivates the search for an alternative form of the GND that can accommodate torus-invariant varieties, a goal that we aim to achieve in a companion paper that we are currently preparing. discrete symmetries, such as subgroups of $O_8$ or $S_8$, with parity and charge-conjugation symmetry accounted for through the application of higher-casing operators in the quasiclassical theory. This approach allows a comprehensive treatment of superconducting order parameters that respect these discrete symmetries, encompassing a wide range of possibilities within these symmetry frameworks. To this end, we created the PROSODY-SEM corpus, a unique dataset that links speech prosody to the meaning of spoken language. We also discovered that modifying the classification method using contextual information can enhance performance and proposed two possible approaches to achieve this. The experiments conducted not only validated the proposed method but also confirmed its potential for use in tasks beyond sentence classification, such as answering questions about the meaning of spoken language. The paper concludes by outlining the implications of these findings and suggesting avenues for further research to advance our understanding of the connection between speech prosody and the meaning of spoken language. To improve performance in such scenarios, we've created a system called Exponential Timed Non-Atomic-Or-Else (ETNAO), which builds upon the existing Non-Atomic-Or-Else (NAO) framework. NAO relies on a central component to manage and execute a series of operations in a transactionally-safe manner. In our ETNAO design, multiple transaction managers can collaborate to perform these operations, significantly expanding the scope of supported transactions. Furthermore, we allow for the rapid creation of short-lived, highly-complex transactions, while also optimizing performance by limiting the size of transactions and their duration. ETNAO is evaluated through two practical implementations and one theoretical model, which demonstrate its capabilities to efficiently manage transactions of varying sizes and durations. Additionally, we outline a strategy for transaction managers to determine the optimal transaction size and duration, thereby enabling a balance between performance and safety in the ETNAO framework. This balance is achieved by considering factors like transaction size, duration, and the associated gas costs, all within compliance with the existing Ethereum gas limit. In our performance analysis, we examine the gas consumption of ETNAO transactions and find them to be a viable option for various use cases, including smart contracts, applications like decentralized data processing, and more. In a comparison of two practical ETNAO implementations, we find that the framework not only meets but actually exceeds the existing performance standards set by NAO transaction managers. This superior performance comes at a cost, however, as the gas consumption of ETNAO transactions is found to be higher than that of basic UTS. In our final analysis, we outline potential future improvements to the ETNAO framework, including the integration with other advanced Ethereum features like dynamic gas pricing, and one potential replacement of NAO transaction managers, all aimed at further enhancing the security and efficiency of the ETNAO design. This research on ETNAO is expected to contribute positively to the development of efficient and secure smart contracts on Ethereum. In addition, the framework may potentially be adapted for use in other blockchain platforms as well. Although impedance control facilitates the development of humanoid robots, it does not provide direct joint torque commands necessary for efficient computation. To resolve this issue, a feedforward force control system is proposed, which utilizes impedance characteristics. The system's stability is ensured through the use of linearized stability analysis based on the Impedance Control Law. To facilitate high-speed calculations, the feedforward control law is developed using the Dynamic Matrix: Response and Force, which enables efficient computation of joint torque responses to ground reaction forces. Addressing this issue, we present the Object Classification Consistency Metric (OCOM), which measures the reliability of object classification models by analyzing both predicted class and subcategory information.  OCOM calculates a consistency score for each class and subcategory by determining the predicted label for a given input using multiple model predictions and then evaluating the similarity between these predicted labels and ground truth labels through a normalized version of the Wagner Transform distance.  We show that lower scores indicate higher prediction confidence, demonstrating the metric's capability to differentiate between accurate and inaccurate predictions.  Furthermore, we reveal that a model's consistency scores can serve as a feature for machine learning performance prediction, achieving a 81.1% success rate in distinguishing between highly reliable and unreliable predictions across multiple models.  We also explore the relationship between prediction confidence and model performance, uncovering a positive correlation and demonstrating that predicting category "dog" versus "cat vs. dog" contributes significantly more to model accuracy than predicting between more specific subcategories like the Bulldog and Shih Tzu subcategories. , Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN have significantly improved object detection accuracy and have become the new baseline for comparison in the field of computer vision. However, these methods have slow processing speeds due to the necessity of classifying each proposal individually. The introduction of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) has made it possible to share information across different proposals, thereby reducing the need for individual classification and increasing processing efficiency. Our method, called S-CNN, utilizes spatial constraints to link related proposals and enables the network to learn proposal correlations through repeated refinement, thereby pinpointing the most accurate proposal for each object. By leveraging these correlations and spatial constraints, S-CNN achieves higher detection accuracy and faster processing speeds compared to RCNN and GCN. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the Pascal VOC2007 dataset and provide a public code repository for easy access. To what extent these internal shifts affect a star's global rotation speed remains unknown. To investigate this, we analyzed data from the Kepler mission for a sample of 15 slowly rotating stars that exhibit X-ray activity. We discovered that those stars' rotation periods range from 103 to 457 days and found that their X-ray cycles are either unaligned with their global rotation, or the evidence is inconclusive. We believe this is likely due to the stars' non-uniform surface rotation speeds, as our models show that a differential rotation pattern similar to the one observed on the Sun is required to explain the observed patterns. Our results imply that a significant number of active stars with surface rotation periods less than 40 days may exist, but are likely going undetected because their cycles would fall within the noise level in current surveys. We also suggest that future missions, such as the PLATO space telescope, are likely to detect these elusive cycles. We further report that a star, KIC 11193715, exhibits not only X-ray activity, but also a drop in brightness and a change in spectral type depending on its rotation cycle, indicating that its surface composition may shift due to changes in its internal magnetic architecture. Finally, we note that additional studies are needed to better understand the relationship between a star's mass and its global rotation speed. Ultimately, these findings contribute to a more comprehensive picture of stellar global activity and set the groundwork for future research with the PLATO mission and other exoplanet hunting projects. learning involves training model parameters on an individual's data or data similar to theirs. However, this often results in models that are only competent for that specific individual, failing to account for the broader personalization context. Existing methods are limited in their ability to adapt to more complex personalization factors such as users' interests and the characteristics of their surrounding environment. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that utilizes self-supervised learning to create robust and personalized models, capable of withstanding uncertainty in various situations. Our approach involves incorporating multiple sources of uncertainty, allowing the models to adapt and generalize better from their unique data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by utilizing it to develop personalized models for two applications: personalized visual reenactment and image generation based on multiple input sources. The former involves learning to regenerate a person's facial structure based on their eyes and a novel image, while the latter involves generating a person's facial structure based on a single image. Both applications are tailored to an individual's specific data or data similar to theirs, while also accounting for the characteristics of their surrounding environment. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach over existing methods through comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Specifically, we show that our approach results in more efficient and effective model training, as well as higher image quality and more consistent results compared to existing methods. Additionally, we show that our approach is versatile and can be applied to a variety of other personalization applications with similar success. Finally, we show that our approach has various potential uses beyond personalization, such as image generation and video generation, while also exploring potential future research directions. Specifically, we show that our approach can be used to generate more realistic images and videos, while also allowing for more efficient model training and more control over the models. Finally, we show that our approach can be used to explore an unbounded video space, while also accounting for an individual's specific data or data similar to theirs, and the characteristics of their surrounding environment.   The substandard pharmaceutical network typically begins with the final product, distributed through complex and often unknown systems.
  By collecting open-source information, researchers can gather insights into these distribution networks, however, the available data usually lacks spatial context.
  Utilizing social media data, researchers can obtain spatially-aware data, but such data is often unverified and subject to biases.
  Another approach involves tracing the flow of pharmaceuticals backwards from reported cases, but this method is restricted to countries with accessible and reliable reporting systems.
  There are a few instances where researchers successfully combined multiple data sources to study health-related issues, but no such method exists for the specific case of pharmaceutical networks.
  Therefore, we introduce the model "MultiSource Pharmaceutical Network Inference" (MPNI), which can combine various types of data to infer pharmaceutical networks.
  We test MPNI using simulated networks and real-world data, highlighting its capacity to handle both single and multiple types of data.
  Furthermore, we address the issue of dealing with missing data within the network and propose a data augmentation strategy to counteract its impact, particularly when working with real-world datasets.
  We evaluate our proposed method by comparing it with alternative network inference models and visualisation tools such as NetworkX, igraph, and visualisation methods like Matplotlib and Plotly, demonstrating its effectiveness. 
  Finally, we outline potential future research directions for MPNI. 
  We believe MPNI has the potential to contribute to our understanding of pharmaceutical networks and enable researchers to identify previously unknown connections.

The study of cosmic rays, through the European Moonshine experiment, specifically looks at searching for signs of muon-electron conversion in space, a sign of new physics that could be indicative of a muon seeing a charged antiparticle and being drawn to it. The European Moonshine experiment has set an ambitious goal of observing 10 conversion events per year, a number that's currently out of reach for current technology. This tool would utilize a series of filters to eliminate unneeded data, beginning with the elimination of events outside the desired muon-e+ direction, followed by removing events containing penetrating radiation, then eliminating events not matching the expected muon-e+ spectrum, and finally using a neural network to filter out remaining background. In contrast, classical importance sampling techniques often struggle to effectively utilize high-dynamic range lights, resulting in either under-exposed or over-exposed scene regions. Our proposed solution, Decoupled Shading and Visibility (DSV), tackles this complex issue by separating the calculation of visibility and shading to accommodate a wide range of light types, including point, directional, and area lights. This enables our approach to maintain both high accuracy and photorealism, as evidenced by our comparisons with state-of-the-art rendering methods, including two highly optimized importance sampling methods. Our results show that DSV not only surpasses these methods in terms of overall image quality but also yields more consistent and accurate results. Furthermore, we explore several potential acceleration strategies, including optimization techniques and efficient sampling methods, to minimize the computational overhead of our approach. Ultimately, our findings indicate that DSV offers a more versatile and reliable solution for high dynamic range lighting that can be applied to a range of rendering methods.
